summary: Gives guidance on reports about interoperation and implementation needed to advance a protocol to Draft Standard. It updates the earlier process because past reports varied widely in form. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary:
Before a protocol can move to Draft Standard in the IETF standards process, someone has to show that separate implementations of it actually work together. That evidence is written up as an implementation report.

The problem was that these reports differed so much that the IESG could not tell a convincing one from an empty one. This RFC says what a report must contain, which parts are optional, and gives a simple outline that most reports can follow. It also relaxes a few demands from RFC 2026, so that writing a useful report is less work.

questions: how to advance to draft standard
what must an interoperability report contain
what is the ietf draft standard requirement
subtitle: What a good implementation report has to contain before a protocol can advance to Draft Standard.

tldr.problem: A protocol can only advance to Draft Standard when two independent implementations have been shown to work together, but the reports submitted as evidence have varied wildly in length and content, and some have proved nothing at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists what a report must identify, what it may leave out, and gives a short outline of sections, from a summary through methodology to exceptions, that most reports can follow in part or in full.
tldr.outcome: Reports become easier to write and easier to judge, because the bar is stated once. The document relaxes several requirements of RFC 2026 while keeping the requirement to demonstrate interoperability.

facts.value: Title, Author, Summary, Methodology, Exceptions, Detail, Appendix

today: RFC 5657 is a Best Current Practice that has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 2026, relaxing some of that document's requirements for implementation reports while keeping the requirement to demonstrate interoperability.

sections.title: Why Reports Needed Guidance
sections.content:
The Draft Standard level and the requirements for standards to meet it are described in RFC 2026. For Draft Standard, not only must two implementations interoperate, but documentation, in the form of the report, must also be provided to the IETF. RFC 2026 puts the responsibility on the Working Group chair: the chair is responsible for documenting the specific implementations which qualify the specification for Draft or Internet Standard status, along with documentation about testing of the interoperation of these implementations. The documentation must include information about the support of each of the individual options and features, and should be submitted to the Area Director with the protocol action request.

Moving documents along the standards track can be an important signal to the user and implementor communities, and the process of submitting a standard for advancement can help improve that standard or the quality of implementations that take part. However, the barriers seem to be high for advancement to Draft Standard, or at the very least confusing.

Having and demonstrating sufficient interoperability is a gating requirement for advancing a protocol to Draft Standard. The primary goal of an implementation report is therefore to convince the IETF and the IESG that the protocol is ready for Draft Standard. That goal can be met by summarising the interoperability characteristics and providing just enough detail to support the conclusion. Side benefits may accrue, such as bugs found or fixed in tested implementations, documentation that can help future implementors, or ideas for other documents.

The level of detail in reports accepted in the past has varied widely. An example of a submitted report that is not sufficient for demonstrating interoperability is, in its entirety: a partial list of implementations including Cray SGI Netstar, IBM HP Network Systems and Convex. That report does not state how it is known that these implementations interoperate, and does not capture whether implementors were asked about features that proved problematic. At the other extreme, reports have been submitted with a great deal of detail about test methodology but relatively little information about what worked and what failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The evidence has to show that two independently written implementations actually talk to each other. Past reports ranged from a bare list of vendor names to long accounts of test methods, and neither extreme told the IESG much.

sections.title: Content Requirements
sections.content:
The implementation report MUST identify the author of the report, who is responsible for characterising the interoperability quality of the protocol. The report MAY identify other contributors, such as testers, those who answered surveys, or those who contributed information, to share credit or blame. It MAY provide a list of report reviewers who corroborate the characterisation of interoperability quality, or name an active working group that reviewed the report.

Some of the requirements of RFC 2026 are relaxed by this update. The report MAY name exactly which implementations were tested, though identifying implementations usually helps meet the goals of implementation reports, and if a subset was tested or surveyed it would help to explain how that subset was chosen or self-selected. The report author MAY choose an appropriate level of detail to document feature interoperability rather than document each individual feature. A contributor other than a working group chair MAY submit an implementation report to an Area Director. Optional features that are not implemented, but are important and do not harm interoperability, MAY, exceptionally and with approval of the IESG, be left in a protocol at Draft Standard.

On independence of implementations: independent implementations should be written by different people at different organisations using different code and protocol libraries. If it is necessary to relax that definition, it can be relaxed as long as there is evidence to show that success is due more to the quality of the protocol than to out-of-band understandings or common code. If there are only two implementations of an undeployed protocol, the report SHOULD identify the implementations and their genealogy, meaning which libraries were used or where the codebase came from. If there are many more implementations, or the protocol is in broad deployment, it is not necessary to call out which two implementations demonstrated interoperability of each given feature, since a reader may conclude that at least some of the implementations of that feature are independent.

On the granularity of features: the granularity of features described in a specification is necessarily very detailed, but the granularity of an implementation report need not be. A report need not list every MUST, SHOULD and MAY in a complete matrix across implementations. A more effective approach might be to characterise the interoperability quality and testing approach, then call out any known problems in either testing or interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: One person must be named as responsible for the report. Naming the implementations, listing every optional feature, or having the working group chair submit it are all now optional, as long as the report still shows that independent implementations work together.

sections.title: The Shape of a Report
sections.content:
The format of implementation and interoperability reports MUST be ASCII text with line breaks for readability. As with Internet-Drafts, no 8-bit characters are currently allowed. It is acceptable, but not necessary, for a report to be formatted as an Internet-Draft.

The document gives a simple outline that an implementation report MAY follow in part or in full. The Title should contain one or more RFC numbers so it can be found in a simple archive, and the name or a common mnemonic of the standard; an example might read "Implementation Report for the Example Name of Some Protocol (ENSP) RFC XXXX". The Author section identifies the author of the report. The Summary attests that the standard meets the requirements for Draft Standard and names who is attesting it, describes how many implementations were tested or surveyed, quickly characterises the deployment level and where the standard can be found in deployment, calls out and, if possible, briefly describes any notably difficult or poorly interoperable features and explains why these still meet the requirement, and asserts any derivative conclusions, such as that if a high-level system is tested and shown to work, then the normative requirements of that system, including all sub-system or lower-layer protocols to the extent a range of features is used, have also been shown to work. The Methodology section describes how the information in the report was obtained, and should be no longer than the summary.

The Exceptions section might read "Every feature was implemented, tested, and widely interoperable without exception and without question". If that statement is not true, the section should cover whether any features were thought to be problematic. Problematic features need not disqualify a protocol from Draft Standard, but this section should explain why they do not, for example because they are optional, untestable, trace or extension features. Detail sections can hold any other justifying or background information, including anything that would have made the summary or methodology sections longer than a few paragraphs, and it would be good to discuss how the considerations sections of the specification played out: were the security considerations accurate and dealt with appropriately, was real internationalisation experience found among the tested implementations, did the implementations have common monitoring or management functionality, and did the IANA registries work as intended. Appendix sections are optional: it is not necessary to archive test suites, test documents, questionnaire text or questionnaire responses, but if it is easy to preserve this information, appendix sections let readers skip over it, can help people doing similar or follow-on reports, and can help new implementors.
sections.plainLanguage: A report is plain text. The outline is short: say who wrote it, summarise what was tested and what the result was, describe how it was tested, list anything that did not work, and put the long material in detail sections and appendices.

sections.title: Choosing the Level of Detail
sections.content:
What constitutes a feature for the purposes of an interoperability report has been frequently debated. Good judgement is required in finding a level of detail that adequately demonstrates coverage of the requirements. Statements made at too high a level result in a document that cannot be verified and that has not adequately challenged whether the testing accidentally missed an important failure to interoperate. On the other hand, statements at too fine a level result in an exponentially exploding matrix of requirement interaction that overburdens the testers and report writers, and the important information in the resulting report would be hard to find in the sea of detail.

The best interoperability reports organise statements of interoperability at a level of detail just sufficient to convince the reader that testing has covered the full set of requirements, and in particular that the testing was sufficient to uncover any places where interoperability does not exist. Reports similar to the one for RTP and RTCP are more useful than an exhaustive checklist of every normative statement in the specification. Each entry in such a report names an interoperability statement and marks it PASS with the implementations tested, or FAIL with an explanation.

Consensus can be a good tool to help determine the appropriate level for such feature descriptions. A working group can make a strong statement by documenting its consensus that a report sufficiently covers a specification and that interoperability has been demonstrated.
sections.plainLanguage: The report should say just enough to prove the requirements were covered. Listing every requirement in a table across every implementation buries the useful information; saying only "it all worked" cannot be checked.

sections.title: Special Cases
sections.content:
For a deployed protocol, results obtained from laboratory testing are not as useful to the IETF as learning what is actually working in deployment. It may therefore be more informative to survey implementors or operators. A questionnaire or interview can elicit information from a wider number of sources. As long as it is known that independent implementations can work in deployment, it is more useful to discover what problems exist than to gather long and detailed checklists of features and options.

For an undeployed protocol, it is appropriate to provide finer-grained detail in reports, because some complicated, flexible or powerful features might show interoperability problems when testers start to probe outside the core use cases. RFC 2026 requires sufficient successful operational experience before progressing a standard to Draft, and notes that Draft Standard may still require additional or more widespread field experience. When possible, reports for protocols without much deployment experience should anticipate common operational considerations, for example putting additional emphasis on overload or congestion management features the protocol may have.

Standards that are not on-the-wire protocols may be special cases. The IESG SHOULD use judgement about what kind of implementation information is acceptable for these kinds of standards. ABNF is an example of a language for which an implementation report was filed: it is interoperable in that protocols are specified using ABNF and these protocols can be successfully implemented and syntax verified. Implementations of ABNF include the RFCs that use it as well as ABNF checking software. Management Information Base modules are sometimes documented in implementation reports as well.

Multiple contributors and multiple reports may be submitted to the sponsoring Area Director one by one. Each report might cover one implementation, including its identification, an affirmation that the implementation works in testing or better in deployment, whether any features are known to interoperate poorly with other implementations, which optional or required features are not implemented, and who is submitting the report. These SHOULD be collated into one document for archiving under one title, but can be concatenated trivially even if the result has several summary sections or introductions.

Some automated tests, such as automated test clients, do not test interoperability directly. When specialised test implementations are necessary, tests can at least be constructed from real-world protocol or document examples. ABNF itself was tested by combining real-world examples, uses of ABNF found in well-known RFCs, and feeding those examples into ABNF checkers, which served as both a deployment proof and an interoperability proof. Atom clients might be tested by finding that they consistently display the information in a test Atom feed built from real-world examples. MIB modules can be tested with generic MIB browsers, to confirm that different implementations return the same values for objects under similar conditions. As a counter-example, the WebDAV test client Litmus is of limited use in demonstrating interoperability for WebDAV because it tests completeness of server implementations and simple test cases, not real-world use or whether real WebDAV clients implement a feature properly or at all.

Optional and extensibility features need not be shown to be implemented everywhere, but they do need to be implemented somewhere, and more than one independent implementation is required. If an optional feature does not meet this requirement, the implementation report must say so and explain why the feature must be kept anyway rather than being evidence of a poor-quality standard. Extensibility points and versioning features are particularly likely to need this kind of treatment, because when a protocol version 1 is released the version field itself is likely to be unused, and before any other versions exist it cannot really be demonstrated that the field is implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The evidence should match the protocol. For something already deployed, ask operators what breaks. For something new, look hard at the awkward features. For a format rather than a protocol, test that parsers agree with each other.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Some good, extremely brief examples of implementation reports can be found in the IETF archives, for the PPP LCP extensions and for OTP. In some cases, perfectly good implementation reports are longer than necessary but may preserve helpful information.

The minimal example given is a report on SMTP pipelining. A large number of SMTP implementations support it, including Innosoft's PMDF and Sun's SIMS, ISODE and MessagingDirect's PP, ISOCOR's nPlex, software.com's post.office, Zmailer, Smail, and the SMTP server in Windows 2000. SMTP pipelining has been widely deployed in these and other implementations for some time, and there have been no reported interoperability problems. Because there were no interoperability problems, the report could provide all the key information in a very terse format, and a reader can infer from the different vendors and platforms that the codebases are, by and in large, independent. The report would only be slightly improved by a positive affirmation that there have been probes or investigations asking about interoperability problems rather than merely a lack of problem reports, and by stating who provided the summary report.

The second example shows how exceptions are covered. The RFC 2821bis SMTP implementation survey asked implementors what features were not implemented. The VRFY and EXPN commands showed up frequently as not implemented or disabled. That report might have justified the interoperability of those features up front, or in an exceptions section, by explaining that EXPN is an optional feature and its support is never relied on, and that VRFY is required but in practice is not relied on because servers can legitimately reply with a non-response. Those commands should remain in the standard because they are sometimes used by administrators within a domain under controlled circumstances, so the occasional utility argues for keeping them, while the lack of problems for end-users means the interoperability of SMTP in real use is not degraded.
sections.plainLanguage: A good report can be one paragraph long when the protocol has been deployed for years and nothing has gone wrong. When something was left unimplemented, the report says so and explains why that does not hurt anyone in practice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This memo introduces no new security considerations. It does note, in the outline of a report, that the detail sections should record how the considerations sections of the specification played out, including whether the security considerations were accurate and were dealt with appropriately in the implementations that were tested.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own. It does ask that a report say whether the security section of the specification held up in practice.

viz.caption: THE REPORT OUTLINE SUGGESTED BY RFC 5657

items.title: Title
items.text: Should contain an RFC number and the name or mnemonic of the standard.

items.title: Author
items.text: Identifies the person responsible for the report.

items.title: Summary
items.text: Attests the standard meets Draft Standard, names who attests, and characterises deployment and any difficult features.

items.title: Methodology
items.text: How the information was obtained. No longer than the summary.

items.title: Exceptions
items.text: Any features that were problematic, and why they do not stop the protocol advancing.

items.title: Detail sections
items.text: Background and justification, including how the specification's own considerations sections played out.

items.title: Appendix sections
items.text: Optional test material and questionnaire material, kept out of the way of readers.

viz.caption: TWO KINDS OF PROTOCOL, TWO KINDS OF EVIDENCE

left.title: Deployed protocol
left.desc: Survey implementors and operators about what is really working, and discover what problems exist.

right.title: Undeployed protocol
right.desc: Give finer-grained detail, probing outside the core use cases and anticipating operational concerns.
